topic: India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA)

subtopics.title: Scope and Entry into Force
subtopics.summary: The India-UK CETA came into force on 15 July 2026, together with the Double Contribution Convention. The booklet calls it a next-generation free trade agreement that goes beyond conventional tariff reduction to cover market access, regulatory transparency and economic partnership. Its coverage spans goods and services, digital trade, investment, government procurement, labour, environment, innovation, SMEs and regulatory cooperation. It is also the first Indian FTA to give tariff concessions on imported passenger vehicles through tariff rate quotas.
facts: CETA and the Double Contribution Convention came into force on 15 July 2026.
CETA is a next-generation FTA that goes beyond conventional tariff reduction.
Coverage includes trade in goods and services, digital trade and investment.
Also covers government procurement, labour, environment, innovation, SMEs and regulatory cooperation.
Addresses market access, regulatory transparency and economic partnership.
First Indian FTA to give tariff concessions on imported passenger vehicles through tariff rate quotas.
The quota approach protects domestic industry while allowing phased market access.

subtopics.title: Tariff Cuts and Market Access
subtopics.summary: India plans to cut duties on 90% of tariff lines, with 85% becoming tariff-free within 10 years. Indian exports get zero-duty access for 99% of products, while auto import tariffs fall to 10% under a quota system from over 100%. Whisky and gin tariffs drop from 150% to 75% and reduce to 40% by the 10th year. The deal also adds 100 annual visas for Indian professionals, and bilateral trade of USD 56.8 billion is expected to double by 2030.
facts: India plans to cut duties on 90% of tariff lines.
85% of tariff lines become tariff-free in 10 years.
Zero-duty access for 99% of Indian exports to the UK.
Auto import tariffs cut to 10% under the quota system, down from over 100%.
Whisky and gin tariffs cut from 150% to 75%, reducing to 40% by the 10th year.
100 additional annual visas for Indian professionals.
Bilateral trade of USD 56.8 billion (GBP 42.6 billion), expected to double by 2030.
UK is India's 4th largest export destination; India ranks 11th as UK's trading partner.
Data exclusivity is excluded from the FTA to safeguard India's generic pharma sector.

subtopics.title: Double Contribution Convention
subtopics.summary: The Double Contribution Convention came into force along with CETA and is aimed at social security contributions. Eligible Indian professionals and employers are exempt from UK National Insurance contributions for up to 5 years. The exemption applies provided contributions continue in India. The purpose is to ensure professionals avoid paying social security contributions in both India and the UK.
facts: India and UK signed the Double Contribution Convention Agreement.
Exempts eligible Indian professionals from paying UK National Insurance contributions.
Exempts eligible Indian employers from paying UK National Insurance contributions.
The exemption covers up to 5 years.
Condition: social security contributions must continue in India.
Purpose: professionals avoid paying social security contributions in both India and UK.
Came into force on 15 July 2026 along with CETA.

subtopics.title: Brexit and Trade Realignment
subtopics.summary: The India-UK FTA is part of Britain's post-Brexit strategy. The UK joined the EU in 1973 and formally left it on 31 January 2020, losing EU market access in the process. The UK and other western nations are diversifying trade away from China, with India as a China-plus-one alternative. India also moved away from RCEP towards bilateral FTAs such as the UK deal.
facts: The UK joined the EU in 1973, when it was known as the European Economic Community.
A referendum held in June 2016 saw around 17.4 million people opt for Brexit.
The UK formally left the EU on 31 January 2020, ending 47 years of membership.
A transition period under the withdrawal agreement ran until the end of 2020.
Brexit meant loss of EU market access, so the UK sought new trade partnerships.
UK and Western nations diversify trade away from China, with India as China-plus-one alternative.
India exited RCEP over trade concerns and shifted focus to bilateral FTAs such as the UK deal.
US tariffs and geopolitical tensions push nations toward stable and predictable trade relations.
The India-UK FTA offers a stable trade framework for economic predictability and long-term growth.

quizzes.passage: The India-UK agreement was pursued in a changing trade environment. After Brexit, the UK lost its access to the EU market and began seeking new trade partnerships for growth and global market access. India's growing economy positions it as a key trade partner for the UK after Brexit. Many Western nations have also moved to diversify their trade away from China, citing supply chain and geopolitical concerns. Under this approach, India is treated as a China-plus-one alternative, and a free trade agreement is central to the diversification strategy. India is also seeking to diversify its trade partners and reduce its dependence on China. Its bilateral free trade agreements, including the one with the UK, are presented as a way to safeguard its interests. Global uncertainty adds to the case. US tariffs and geopolitical tensions are pushing nations towards stable and predictable trade relations. The agreement is described as offering a stable trade framework that ensures economic predictability and long-term growth amid that uncertainty. The agreement itself is described as a next-generation free trade agreement. It goes beyond conventional tariff reduction, and the booklet presents it as a framework for wider economic partnership. Its coverage is wide, and it is presented as a step in India's broader trade realignment.

quizzes.passage: A trade pact between two countries has been described as a next-generation free trade agreement. It goes beyond conventional tariff reduction and deals with market access, regulatory transparency and economic partnership. Its scope covers trade in goods and services, digital trade, investment, government procurement, labour, environment, innovation, SMEs and regulatory cooperation. Alongside the trade pact, the two countries signed a Double Contribution Convention Agreement. The Convention sits alongside the pact as a separate instrument. The booklet discusses it in a separate box alongside the trade pact. Wider context in the booklet relates to these trade arrangements. After leaving the EU, the UK lost its access to the EU market and sought new trade partnerships for growth and global market access. Western nations have also moved to diversify trade away from China because of supply chain and geopolitical concerns. US tariffs and geopolitical tensions have pushed nations towards stable and predictable trade relations. The booklet presents such pacts as offering economic predictability and long-term growth amid global uncertainty, and it describes the wider Brexit background as the UK leaving the European Union, an economic and political union of 28 European countries. It allows free trade among member countries without any checks or extra charges. Britain has faced many more challenges while sacrificing the smooth and frictionless flow of goods across its borders.
